title: the summit sit
hook: a woman stands in a king's hall with his son, he says he doesn't remember her, and she doesn't leave quietly

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to Ayurveda, and an old definition of health that doesn't stop at the body. Did you do one small thing toward what well would look like? Today, a new week on the summit, and a hall full of people. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `A NEW WEEK ON THE SUMMIT.`

segments.voice: A royal hall, crowded. A woman walks in from the forest with a small boy beside her. She reminds the king of his promise. The king looks straight at her and says he doesn't remember her. In the Mahabharata, Shakuntala stands there, stunned and furious. And then she speaks, at length, in his own hall, in front of everyone. That scene came near the end of a long stretch of this year, when the path went back to the epics and listened to the women in them. Today's summit sit returns to that stretch and hears those women all at once.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE KING'S HALL.` → `I DO NOT REMEMBER YOU.` → `SHE DOESN'T LEAVE QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: Line them up and something stands out. The epics give these women words, often at the very moment someone expects them to be silent. Sita, told to stay home while Rama goes into exile, argues with him: from duty, from love, and, Valmiki keeps it, with a sharp line about whether her father married her to a man at all. She wins. She goes. Gandhari's son comes to her during the war asking a blessing of victory, and she won't say the words he wants. She gives him a line that refuses to take sides by name: where dharma is, there is victory. Savitri walks behind Death on the road, with no weapon and no army, only a conversation. In the epic, what pleases Yama is not her grief or her cleverness. It's what she says about the good. Kunti, in the Bhagavata, asks Krishna for a strange gift: let the troubles come again, because in trouble she saw him. Damayanti, searching for a husband who vanished, doesn't send soldiers. She sends a question only he would understand. And Shakuntala, denied in that crowded hall, tells the king that the sun and the moon and his own heart all saw what he did. Now turn it. Readers hear these women differently, and the tradition holds the readings side by side. Some hear devotion first: loyalty, faith, steadiness under loss. Others hear women choosing their own road, sometimes against the men trying to choose it for them. Some readers notice retellings that make them quieter than the old texts do. The texts themselves keep the lines. That's the view from the top of this stretch. Not one woman, and not one lesson. A row of voices, each speaking at the hour it cost the most to speak.
screen: `THE EPICS GIVE THEM WORDS.` · `SITA ARGUES, GANDHARI WON'T FLATTER.` · `SAVITRI TALKS ON THE ROAD WITH DEATH.` · `THE READINGS HELD SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `A ROW OF VOICES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a row of voices, heard in quiet. Sit, and let the breath settle into its own pace. Let one of these women come to mind, whichever arrives first. Don't study her. Just let her stand there, at the moment she spoke. Then notice, gently, whether there's a true thing you've been keeping quiet about. You don't have to say it. Just let it be known to you, the way the sun and the moon saw. If you pray, you can bring it before God, or before the goddess, in words you already know. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: the women of the epics, each given words at the hardest hour. Today's word.
Your line: the summit sit. Today, when you hear a story told about a woman, ask once: what did she actually say? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: The women of the epics are remembered in retellings, songs, plays and household observances; Savitri, for example, is remembered by some married Hindu women in a vow kept at a banyan tree.

fork.setup: you're Kunti. Krishna's chariot is ready to leave, and he'll grant you a gift. you've lived through poison, exile and war. what do you ask for?
options: peace and comfort for the rest of your life.
a kingdom for each of your sons.
fork.reveal: in the Bhagavata, Kunti asks for the troubles to come again and again, because in trouble she saw Krishna.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: dharma, the word in Gandhari's line, where dharma is, there is victory.

trapdoor: what you thought: the women of the epics are patient, silent wives.
what it means: the texts give them words, often at the very moment someone expects them to be silent.

what a scholar hears: Sita's argument in the Ayodhya Kanda, Gandhari's yato dharmas tato jayah, and Shakuntala's speech of witnesses in the Adi Parva, read as devotion by some and as women choosing their own road by others.
